E1.text_clean:
E1. This question is about stars.
The Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram shows the Sun, a star labelled A and the main sequence.
[Diagram: HR diagram, absolute magnitude (−10 to 15, decreasing upwards) against spectral class O B A F G K M; grey main sequence band; the Sun at magnitude ≈5, class G; star A at magnitude ≈1, class G, above the main sequence]
(a) (i) Define absolute magnitude. [1]
(ii) State one physical property of a star that is determined by its spectral class. [1]
(iii) Suggest why star A has a greater radius than the Sun. [1]
(b) Star A is part of a binary star system. The diagram shows the orbit of star A and the orbit of its companion, star B.
[Diagram: concentric circular orbits; star B on the outer orbit moving up, star A on the inner orbit moving down; Earth is to the right]
The temperature of star A is $T_A$, the temperature of star B is $T_B$ and $\frac{T_A}{T_B}=0.60$. The radius of star A is $R_A$, the radius of star B is $R_B$ and $\frac{R_A}{R_B}=270$.
(i) Show that the luminosity of star A is $9.4\times10^{3}$ times greater than the luminosity of star B. [2]
(ii) Draw the approximate position of star B onto the HR diagram on page 2. [1]
(c) The diagram below shows the spectrum of the stars as observed from Earth. The spectrum shows one line from star A and one line from star B, when the stars are in the position shown in the diagram (b).
[Diagram: spectrum strip with increasing wavelength to the right; line from star B on the left, line from star A near the middle]
On the spectrum draw lines to show the approximate positions of these spectral lines after the stars have completed one quarter of a revolution. [2]

E2.text_clean:
E2. This question is about Cepheid stars.
(a) The star $\eta$ Aquilae is a Cepheid star. Its apparent magnitude varies from 3.6 to 4.4 with a period of 7.2 days.
(i) State the reason for the variation of the Cepheid's brightness. [1]
(ii) The average absolute magnitude $M$ of a Cepheid star and the period $T$ in days of the variation of its brightness are related by the equation below.
$M=-2.83\log_{10}T-1.81$
Determine the distance to $\eta$ Aquilae. [3]
(b) A Cepheid star and non-Cepheid star both belong to the same distant galaxy. Explain, stating the quantities that need to be measured, how the luminosity of the non-Cepheid star may be determined. [2]

E3.text_clean:
E3. This question is about cosmology.
(a) Theoretical studies indicate that the universe may be open, closed or flat.
(i) State, by reference to critical density, the condition that must be satisfied for the universe to be flat. [1]
(ii) In a flat universe, the rate of expansion would be slowing down. Suggest a reason for this. [1]
(iii) Outline why it has been difficult to determine whether the universe is open, closed or flat. [2]
(b) Outline one piece of experimental evidence that supports the fact that the universe is expanding. [2]

E4.text_clean:
E4. This question is about stellar evolution.
(a) A main sequence star has a mass of $2.2M_\odot$ where $M_\odot=1$ solar mass. The lifetime of a star on the main sequence is proportional to $\frac{M}{L}$ where $M$ is the mass and $L$ is the luminosity of the star.
Using the mass–luminosity relation $L\propto M^{3.5}$ show that the
(i) luminosity of the star is $16L_\odot$ where $L_\odot=1$ solar luminosity. [1]
(ii) lifetime of this star on the main sequence will be approximately $\frac{1}{7}$ of the lifetime of the Sun. [2]
(b) The star in (a) will evolve to become a white dwarf. The diagram represents the stages in the evolution of the star.
[Diagram: four boxes linked by arrows: main sequence → [blank] → [blank] → white dwarf]
(i) On the diagram, label the two intermediate stages. [2]
(ii) State what may be deduced about the mass of this star when it is in the white dwarf stage. [1]

E5.text_clean:
E5. This question is about Hubble's law.
(a) The fractional change in the wavelength $\lambda$ of light from the galaxy Hydra is $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}=0.204$. The distance to Hydra is 820 Mpc.
Estimate in $\text{km s}^{-1}\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ a value for the Hubble constant. [2]
(b) An estimate of the age of the universe is $\frac{1}{H}$ where $H$ is the Hubble constant. Suggest why $\frac{1}{H}$ overestimates the age of the universe. [2]

F1.text_clean:
F1. This question is about modulation.
The diagram shows the variation with time $t$ of the voltage signal $V$ of an amplitude modulated carrier wave.
[Graph: V / V (−4 to 4) against t / μs (0 to 6); carrier oscillation whose amplitude envelope varies between about 3.2 V (at t ≈ 1 μs and 5 μs) and 0.8 V (at t ≈ 3 μs)]
(a) Determine the
(i) frequency of the carrier wave. [1]
(ii) frequency of the signal (information) wave. [1]
(iii) amplitude of the signal wave. [1]
(b) On the axes below, draw the spectrum of the modulated wave, i.e. the variation with frequency $f$ of the amplitude of the voltage $V$. [2]
[Axes: amplitude of V / arbitrary units against f / MHz, marked 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0]

F2. This question is about digital transmission.
(a) The diagram below is a block diagram for the digital transmission of an analogue signal.
[Block diagram: input analogue signal → X → Y - - - serial-to-parallel converter → DAC → output analogue signal]
(i) State the names of blocks X and Y. [2]
X:
Y:

(b) The diagrams show the variation with time of the input and output analogue signal voltages.
[Graphs: input voltage against time — a smooth varying curve; output voltage against time — a coarse stepped approximation of the input]
State and explain two ways in which the output signal could be made to be a more accurate reproduction of the input signal. [4]

F3.text_clean:
F3. This question is about optic fibres.
(a) State one advantage of the use of an optic fibre rather than a coaxial cable for the transmission of information. [1]
(b) Suggest why, in transmitting information in an optic fibre, infrared electromagnetic radiation rather than visible light is used. [2]
(c) A signal is fed into an optic fibre of length $L$.
[Diagram: input → optic fibre of length L → receiver]
The noise power at the receiver is $P_{noise}=4.2\,\mu\text{W}$. The signal to noise ratio (i.e. $10\log\frac{P_{signal}}{P_{noise}}$) at the receiver must exceed 25 dB.
(i) Show that the minimum signal power at the receiver is 1.3 mW. [1]
(ii) A signal of power 25 mW is input to the optic fibre. The attenuation per unit length of the optic fibre is $0.30\,\text{dB km}^{-1}$. Determine the maximum length $L$ of the optic fibre. [3]

F4.text_clean:
F4. This question is about the operational amplifier (op-amp).
(a) State two properties of an ideal operational amplifier (op-amp). [2]
(b) The diagram shows a circuit that includes an op-amp.
[Circuit: non-inverting amplifier; $V_{IN}$ applied to the + input; feedback resistor R from output to the − input; 4.0 kΩ resistor from the − input to the zero volt line; $V_{OUT}$ measured from output to zero volt line]
The overall gain of this circuit is $\frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}}=26$. Calculate the resistance of resistor $R$. [2]
(c) The op-amp operates with a ±9.0 V supply. Determine the value of the output voltage $V_{OUT}$ for input voltages $V_{IN}$ of
(i) −0.30 V. [1]
(ii) +3.0 V. [1]

F5.text_clean:
F5. This question is about the mobile phone system.
The diagram shows a few of the cells in a mobile phone system. Each cell has its own base station. The base stations are connected to a cellular exchange.
[Diagram: seven hexagonal cells in a honeycomb pattern]
(a) Suggest why the size of each cell is usually limited to no more than a few kilometres. [2]
(b) Describe how, at any one instant, many mobile phones may be communicating with the same base station. [2]

G1.text_clean:
G1. This question is about interference of light at two parallel slits.
(a) State the condition necessary to observe interference between two light sources. [1]
(b) The diagram below shows an arrangement for observing a double slit interference pattern. A parallel beam of coherent light of wavelength 410 nm is incident on two parallel narrow slits separated by 0.30 mm. A screen is placed 1.60 m beyond the slits.
[Diagram: incident light → double slit (separation 0.30 mm) → screen 1.60 m away (not to scale)]
Calculate the fringe spacing on the screen. [2]
(c) The slits in (b) are replaced by a large number of slits of the same width and separation as the double slit. Describe the effects that this change will have on the appearance of the fringes on the screen. [3]

G2.text_clean:
G2. This question is about the simple magnifying glass and the compound microscope.
(a) Define, for the unaided eye, the term near point. [1]
(b) A converging lens is used as a magnifying glass. On the diagram draw rays to construct the image of the object, o. [3]
[Diagram: converging lens on a principal axis with focal points f on each side; small object o between the lens and the right-hand focal point]
(c) The lens has a focal length $f$. When the image is formed at the near point, the distance $u$ of the object from the lens is given by
$u=\frac{fD}{D+f}$
where $D$ is the near point distance.
Deduce that the angular magnification $M$ is given by
$M=1+\frac{D}{f}$. [2]
(d) A compound microscope consists of an eyepiece lens of focal length 6.0 cm and an objective lens of focal length 2.8 cm. An object is placed 3.4 cm from the objective lens and the final image of the object is formed by the microscope at the near point.
Determine the
(i) angular magnification of the eyepiece. Take the near point distance to be 25 cm. [1]
(ii) distance from the objective lens of the intermediate image formed by this lens. [2]
(iii) overall magnification of the compound microscope. [2]

G3.text_clean:
G3. This question is about the scattering of light.
Explain, with reference to the scattering of light, why the sky appears red at sunset. [3]
G3.note: Rayleigh scattering has no dedicated code; tagged C.2 (EM waves/wave model).

G4.text_clean:
G4. This question is about X-rays.
(a) X-rays are produced in an X-ray tube.
(i) State and explain how the continuous and characteristic X-ray spectra are produced. [4]
(ii) Outline how the intensity of the X-rays produced is controlled. [2]
(b) (i) Some X-rays are produced by an accelerating potential of 25 kV. Show that the minimum wavelength of these X-rays is $5.0\times10^{-11}$ m. [2]
(ii) X-rays of wavelength $5.0\times10^{-11}$ m are incident on a crystal. An intense scattered beam is observed at an angle of 19° to a set of lattice planes in the crystal.
[Diagram: incident X-rays at 19° to rows of atoms in lattice planes separated by d; scattered X-rays leaving at 19°]
Calculate the lattice spacing $d$ of these planes. [2]

H1.text_clean:
H1. This question is about relativistic kinematics.
A source of light S and a detector of light D are placed on opposite walls of a box as shown in the diagram.
[Diagram: box with S on the left wall and D on the right wall, L = 6.0 m apart; box moves to the right at v = 0.80c relative to the ground]
According to an observer in the box the distance $L$ between S and D is 6.0 m. The box moves with speed $v=0.80c$ relative to the ground.
Consider the following events.
Event 1: a photon is emitted by S towards D
Event 2: the photon arrives at D
(a) In the context of the theory of relativity, state what is meant by an event. [1]
(b) (i) Calculate the time interval $t$ between event 1 and event 2 according to an observer in the box. [1]
(ii) According to an observer on the ground the time interval between event 1 and event 2 is $T$. One student claims that $T=\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}}$ and another that $T=t\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}$.
Explain why both students are wrong. [2]
(c) Relative to an observer on the ground,
(i) calculate the distance between S and D. [2]
(ii) state the speed of the photon leaving S. [1]
(iii) state an expression for the distance travelled by detector D in the time interval $T$ ($T$ is the interval in (b)(ii)). [1]
(iv) determine $T$, using your answers to (c)(i), (ii) and (iii). [2]
(d) Describe how the Hafele–Keating experiment provides evidence in support of the special theory of relativity. [3]

H2.text_clean:
H2. This question is about rest mass and relativistic energy.
(a) (i) Define the rest mass of a particle. [1]
(ii) The rest mass of a particle is said to be an invariant quantity. State, with reference to special relativity, what is meant by the term invariant. [1]
(b) In a thought experiment, two particles X and Y, each of rest mass $380\,\text{MeV c}^{-2}$, are approaching each other head on.
[Diagram: particle X moving right at 0.60c towards particle Y moving left at 0.60c]
The speed of X and of Y is 0.60c relative to a laboratory.
(i) Calculate the momentum of X in the frame of reference in which Y is at rest. [3]
(ii) As a result of the collision a single particle Z is formed. Determine the rest mass of Z. The gamma factor for a speed of 0.60c is 1.25. [2]

H3.text_clean:
H3. This question about general relativity.
(a) State the principle of equivalence. [1]
(b) A gamma-ray photon is emitted from the base of a tower towards the top of the tower.
[Diagram: tower with a photon travelling upwards from its base]
(i) Explain, using the principle of equivalence, why the frequency of the photon as measured at the top of the tower is less than that measured at the base of the tower. [3]
(ii) The frequency of the photon at the base is $3.5\times10^{18}$ Hz and the tower is 23 m high. Determine the shift $\Delta f$ in the frequency of the photon at the top of the tower. [1]
(iii) Suggest, using your answer to (b)(ii), why the photon frequency must be measured very precisely for this experiment to be successful. [1]

H4.text_clean:
H4. This question is about black holes.
The diagram shows the path of a light ray in the space around a black hole.
[Diagram: black hole with a dotted circle of radius $R_S$; a light ray travels in a straight line far away then curves around near the black hole (not to scale)]
The radius of the dotted circle is the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole.
(a) Define the Schwarzschild radius of a black hole. [1]
(b) Explain, using the concept of spacetime, why the path of the light ray is straight at distances far from the black hole and curved when near the black hole. [3]

I1.text_clean:
I1. This question is about the ear and hearing.
The diagram shows the principal features of the human ear.
[Diagram: cross-section of the human ear showing outer ear, ear canal, middle ear and inner ear]
(a) On the diagram, identify
(i) the cochlea using the letter C. [1]
(ii) the ossicles using the letter O. [1]
(iii) the auditory nerves using the letter A. [1]
(b) For a person with normal hearing
(i) state the range of frequencies that can be heard. [1]
(ii) describe the effect of increasing age on your answer to (b)(i). [2]
(c) Explain what is meant by the fact that the ear has a logarithmic response to changes in sound intensity. [2]
(d) The intensity of sound at the ear of a person is $10^{-6}\,\text{W m}^{-2}$. Determine by how much the intensity of the sound must be increased for the sound intensity level at the ear to be doubled. [3]

I2.text_clean:
I2. This question is about X-rays.
(a) Define the attenuation coefficient as applied to a beam of X-rays travelling through a medium. [2]
(b) Derive the relationship between the attenuation coefficient $\mu$ and the half-value thickness $x_{\frac{1}{2}}$. [2]
(c) Aluminium is often used to filter out the low energy X-rays in a beam of X-rays. The following data are available for a particular X-ray beam.
X-ray energy / keV | half-value thickness of aluminium / mm
15 | 0.70
30 | 3.5
Assuming equal initial intensities, determine, after the X-ray beam has passed through an aluminium sheet 6.0 mm thick, the following ratio. [3]
$\frac{\text{intensity of 15 keV X-rays}}{\text{intensity of 30 keV X-rays}}$
(d) Outline why X-rays are not suitable to image an organ such as the liver. [2]

I3.text_clean:
I3. This question is about the use of radioactive isotopes in medicine.
(a) Distinguish between the biological half-life and effective half-life of a radioactive isotope. [2]
(b) The radioactive isotope iodine-131 undergoes beta decay to the stable isotope xenon-131 with a physical half-life of 8.0 days. Gamma radiation is also emitted in this decay. Iodine-131 is readily absorbed by the thyroid gland. The biological half-life is 21 days.
(i) Calculate the effective half-life of iodine-131. [2]
(ii) Suggest why iodine-131 is often chosen to treat cancer of the thyroid gland. [3]
(c) Iodine-131 can be used to estimate the total blood volume of a patient.
A small amount of the isotope is dissolved in $8.0\,\text{cm}^3$ of a solution. $4.0\,\text{cm}^3$ of this solution is injected into the patient. After a few minutes a $5.0\,\text{cm}^3$ blood sample is taken. The activity of this sample is measured to be 96 Bq.
The remaining $4.0\,\text{cm}^3$ of the solution is mixed with $1000\,\text{cm}^3$ of water. The activity of $5.0\,\text{cm}^3$ of this solution is measured to be 510 Bq.
Estimate the total volume of blood in the patient. [3]

J1.text_clean:
J1. This question is about quarks.
(a) State the name of a particle that is its own antiparticle. [1]
(b) The meson $K^0$ consists of a d quark and an anti s quark. The $K^0$ decays into two pions as shown in the Feynman diagram.
[Feynman diagram: $K^0$ ($\bar{s}$, d) on the left; the $\bar{s}$ line emits a dashed exchange particle and becomes $\bar{d}$; the exchange particle produces u and $\bar{u}$; outputs $\pi^+$ ($\bar{d}$ u) and $\pi^-$ ($\bar{u}$ d)]
(i) State a reason why the kaon $K^0$ cannot be its own antiparticle. [1]
(ii) Explain how it may be deduced that this decay is a weak interaction process. [2]
(iii) State the name of the particle denoted by the dotted line in the diagram. [1]
(iv) The mass of the particle in (b)(iii) is approximately $1.6\times10^{-25}$ kg. Determine the range of the weak interaction. [2]
(c) (i) Explain why the meson $K^0$ does not have any colour quantum number. [2]
(ii) The decay $K^0\to p^+ + \pi^-$ is not observed. State one conservation law that would be violated if this decay were to occur. [1]

Protons are injected into the cyclotron from a source S. The arrow indicates the direction of a proton after it has left the source. The magnetic field is directed into the plane of the page.

(i) State the function of a wire chamber. [1]

(b) Describe how deep inelastic scattering experiments support your answer to (a). [2]
